title: Neusis vs. Compass-Straightedge: The Pierpont Prime Extension
content: Compass-and-straightedge (C&S) constructions allow operations generating square roots: field extensions of degree 2 at each step. This gives the Fermat prime criterion (Gauss-Wantzel): n-gon C&S-constructible iff φ(n) is a power of 2. Neusis (marked ruler) constructions additionally allow conic intersections, generating degree-3 extensions. This extends the constructible class: n-gon neusis-constructible iff φ(n) = 2^u · 3^v (3-smooth), equivalently n = 2^a · 3^b × (distinct Pierpont primes). Gleason (1988) proved this in 'Angle Trisection, the Heptagon, and the Triskaidecagon.' The regular 7-gon is the canonical example: φ(7)=6=2·3 is 3-smooth (neusis-constructible) but 6 is not a power of 2 (not C&S-constructible). This file formalizes the number-theoretic component (Pierpont prime definitions and verification) but notes that the Galois-theoretic geometric step connecting φ(n) being 3-smooth to actual constructibility is not yet formalized.
mathContext: C&S: $\phi(n) = 2^k$ (Fermat prime criterion). Neusis: $\phi(n) = 2^u \cdot 3^v$ (Pierpont prime criterion). The extension class: Fermat primes $\subset$ Pierpont primes (every Fermat prime $p = 2^{2^k}+1$ has $p-1 = 2^{2^k}$, which is 3-smooth). Additional Pierpont primes: $7$ (p-1=6=2·3), $19$ (p-1=18=2·3²), $37$ (p-1=36=4·9), $73$, $97$, $109$, $193$, ...

title: Is23Smooth: 3-Smooth Numbers and Their Properties
content: Is23Smooth n is defined as `0 < n ∧ ∃ a b : ℕ, n = 2^a * 3^b`. This captures exactly the 3-smooth (or 23-smooth) numbers: those whose prime factorization uses only 2 and 3. Fifteen specific 3-smooth numbers are verified: 1 (2⁰·3⁰), 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12, 16, 18, 36, 72, 96, 108, 192 — corresponding to p-1 for the first 12 Pierpont primes. Two non-examples: not_is23Smooth_five proves 5 is not 3-smooth (5|5 but 5≠2,3, proved by prime_factor_not_two_three_of_smooth); not_is23Smooth_ten proves 10 is not 3-smooth (5|10, same helper). The key structural lemma is_23Smooth_mul: 3-smooth is closed under multiplication (concatenating exponents: 2^a·3^b × 2^c·3^d = 2^{a+c}·3^{b+d}). This closure property is what makes the totient condition φ(m)·φ(n) = φ(mn) (for coprime m,n) preserve 3-smoothness — enabling the Pierpont prime criterion to reduce to checking each prime factor.
mathContext: $\text{Is23Smooth}(n) \Leftrightarrow n = 2^a \cdot 3^b$ for some $a,b \geq 0$. OEIS A003586. First few: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12, 16, 18, 24, 27, 32, 36, 48, 54, 64, 72, 81, 96, ... Closed under $\times$: $(2^a 3^b)(2^c 3^d) = 2^{a+c}3^{b+d}$.

title: IsPierpontPrime: Definition and the 12 Verified Examples
content: IsPierpontPrime p is `Nat.Prime p ∧ Is23Smooth (p - 1)`: a prime p such that p-1 = 2^u · 3^v. Each of the 12 verified Pierpont primes is proved as a conjunction of primality (by decide or norm_num) and Is23Smooth (p-1) (by the appropriate is23Smooth_* lemma). The pattern: isPierpontPrime_seven = ⟨by decide, is23Smooth_six⟩ since 7-1=6 and is23Smooth_six : Is23Smooth 6 provides 6=2¹·3¹. Larger primes use norm_num instead of decide (e.g., isPierpontPrime_seventythree: ⟨by norm_num, is23Smooth_seventytwo⟩). The 12 primes with their p-1 factorizations: 2(1), 3(2), 5(4=2²), 7(6=2·3), 13(12=4·3), 17(16=2⁴), 19(18=2·9), 37(36=4·9), 73(72=8·9), 97(96=32·3), 109(108=4·27), 193(192=64·3). Note that 17=2⁴+1 and 5=2²+1 are Fermat primes (powers of 2), while 7=2·3+1 and 19=2·3²+1 are Pierpont primes that are NOT Fermat primes.
mathContext: $p$ Pierpont: $p$ prime and $p-1 = 2^u 3^v$. Note $p-1 = 2^{2^k}$ (Fermat) $\Rightarrow$ $p-1$ is 3-smooth $\Rightarrow$ $p$ is Pierpont. Converse false: $7-1=6=2\cdot 3$ is 3-smooth but $6 \neq 2^k$, so 7 is Pierpont but not Fermat.
relatedConcepts: Fermat prime as special case of Pierpont

title: Non-Pierpont Proofs and Fermat-is-Pierpont via Structural Reasoning
content: Section §4 proves 4 non-examples. Each is_isPierpontPrime proof unifies with ⟨_, h⟩ (discarding the primality component) and then ⟨_, a, b, h⟩ (unfolding Is23Smooth to get n = 2^a · 3^b) and uses prime_factor_not_two_three_of_smooth with the explicit non-2-non-3 prime: 11→not_11 (5|10), 23→not_23 (11|22), 29→not_29 (7|28), 41→not_41 (5|40). Section §5 then proves structural properties. fermatPrime_is_pierpont: if p is prime and p = 2^{2^k}+1 then p is Pierpont, since p-1 = 2^{2^k} = 2^{2^k}·3⁰ is 3-smooth. The proof shows 2^{2^k}+1 - 1 = 2^{2^k} by Nat.add_sub_cancel then exhibits Is23Smooth witness ⟨1, 2^k, 0, by simp⟩. isPierpontPrime_totient_smooth: φ(p) = p-1 for prime p (Nat.totient_prime), so 3-smooth p-1 implies 3-smooth φ(p).
mathContext: Non-examples: $p-1 = 10 = 2\cdot5$ ($5\nmid\{2,3\}$), $22 = 2\cdot11$, $28 = 4\cdot7$, $40 = 8\cdot5$. Fermat: $p = 2^{2^k}+1 \Rightarrow p-1 = 2^{2^k} = 2^{2^k}\cdot3^0$ (3-smooth). $\varphi(p) = p-1$ for prime $p$ (Nat.totient_prime).

title: Neusis Constructibility Table: φ(n) 3-Smooth = n-gon Constructible by Neusis
content: Section §6 verifies the neusis constructibility criterion for 7 specific polygons via their totient smoothness. Totients by native_decide: φ(7)=6, φ(9)=6, φ(13)=12, φ(19)=18, φ(37)=36, φ(11)=10, φ(23)=22. Constructible (3-smooth totient): 7-gon (6=2·3), 9-gon (6=2·3), 13-gon (12=4·3), 19-gon (18=2·9), 37-gon (36=4·9). Not constructible (non-3-smooth totient): 11-gon (10=2·5, has prime factor 5) and 23-gon (22=2·11, has prime factor 11). The proofs use `prime_factor_not_two_three_of_smooth` again for non-examples. The Gleason (1988) criterion states: IsTwoThreeNumber(φ(n)) ↔ n-gon is neusis-constructible — but Gleason's theorem is not formally proved in Lean here; only the number-theoretic verification is done.
mathContext: Neusis-constructible: $\phi(n) = 2^u \cdot 3^v$. Table: 7-gon ($\phi=6$✓), 9-gon ($\phi=6$✓), 13-gon ($\phi=12$✓), 19-gon ($\phi=18$✓), 37-gon ($\phi=36$✓). Not: 11-gon ($\phi=10=2\cdot5$✗), 23-gon ($\phi=22=2\cdot11$✗). Gleason: the 7-gon is the simplest non-C&S-constructible polygon that IS neusis-constructible.

title: Summary: What's Proved vs. What Remains for Full Gleason Theorem
content: The §7 summary documents both achievements and gaps. Proved: (1) 15 specific 3-smooth numbers verified (p-1 values for the 12 Pierpont primes); (2) 12 Pierpont primes verified with explicit witnessing exponents; (3) 4 non-Pierpont primes verified with explicit non-3-smooth witnesses; (4) Totient 3-smoothness for 5 neusis-constructible n-gons and non-smoothness for 2 non-constructible ones. Not proved: the Galois-theoretic connection from φ(n) being 3-smooth to actual geometric neusis-constructibility. This requires (a) Gal(ℚ(ζₙ)/ℚ) ≅ (ℤ/nℤ)* with order φ(n), and (b) that Galois groups decomposable into degree-2 and degree-3 steps correspond to neusis constructions. Mathlib has the cyclotomic Galois machinery (IsCyclotomicExtension) but the geometric constructibility axioms for neusis are not yet in Mathlib.
mathContext: Proved: $\{p \text{ Pierpont} : p \leq 193\}$ and $\{n \text{ s.t. } \phi(n) \text{ is 3-smooth} : n \in \{7,9,13,19,37\}\}$. Missing: Gleason's Galois-theoretic proof that $\phi(n)$ 3-smooth $\Rightarrow$ $n$-gon neusis-constructible (requires axiomatizing neusis constructions in Lean).
